_reviewed_by: Dimple (Medical Safety & Privacy Lead) & Kavya (Knowledge Lead)

general_advice: Ensure adequate physical rest to support recovery.
Drink plenty of fluids such as warm water, herbal teas, or clear broths to stay hydrated.
Use saline nasal sprays or rinses to ease nasal congestion.
Use a cool-mist humidifier or inhale steam from a warm shower to soothe irritated airways.
Gargle with warm salt water to help relieve throat irritation.
when_to_seek_care: Fever lasting more than 3 to 4 days, or fever returning after subsiding.
Shortness of breath, wheezing, or chest discomfort.
Severe sinus headache or facial swelling that persists or worsens.
Inability to swallow fluids or signs of dehydration.
monitoring_tips: Track symptom progression over 7 to 10 days; common cold symptoms typically resolve within this window.
Check body temperature if feeling chills or feverish.

general_advice: Prioritize bed rest and limit physical exertion.
Maintain steady fluid intake with water, oral rehydration solutions, or warm broths.
Rest in a quiet, temperature-regulated room.
Apply a cool, damp washcloth to the forehead to ease feverish discomfort.
when_to_seek_care: Difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, or persistent chest pressure.
Persistent high fever unresponsive to supportive measures.
Confusion, dizziness, or severe lethargy.
Bluish lips or pale skin.
monitoring_tips: Monitor daily fluid intake and ensure regular urination.
Watch for secondary worsening after initial improvement.

general_advice: Rest in a well-ventilated room and separate from others where possible.
Stay well hydrated by sipping water and clear fluids throughout the day.
Rest in prone (lying on stomach) or side-lying positions to improve respiratory comfort if helpful.
Use steam inhalation or lozenges to soothe dry cough or throat irritation.
when_to_seek_care: Trouble breathing, persistent pain or pressure in the chest.
Oxygen saturation falling below 94% on a pulse oximeter if available.
New confusion or inability to wake or stay alert.
Bluish or pale lips, face, or nail beds.
monitoring_tips: Check oxygen saturation and body temperature twice daily if monitoring at home.
Note any sudden shortness of breath during minimal exertion.

general_advice: Gargle with warm salt water (half teaspoon salt in a glass of warm water) several times daily.
Sip warm liquids like herbal tea with honey or clear broths to soothe throat tissue.
Rest your voice and avoid exposure to tobacco smoke or dry indoor air.
Use a cool-mist humidifier near your resting area.
when_to_seek_care: Difficulty swallowing liquids or saliva, or difficulty opening the mouth.
Severe pain lasting longer than 5 to 7 days.
High fever or swollen, tender neck lymph nodes.
Development of a widespread rash or breathing difficulties.
monitoring_tips: Observe throat appearance for white patches or severe swelling.
Check whether swallowing improves or becomes more difficult over 48 hours.

general_advice: Use warm facial compresses over the bridge of the nose and forehead to relieve sinus pressure.
Perform gentle saline nasal irrigations or use sterile saline nasal drops.
Inhale warm steam from a bowl of hot water or a warm shower.
Keep the head elevated while sleeping to promote sinus drainage.
Stay well hydrated to help thin mucus secretions.
when_to_seek_care: Swelling, redness, or pain around one or both eyes.
Severe frontal headache with high fever or stiff neck.
Vision changes, double vision, or confusion.
Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without any improvement.
monitoring_tips: Note whether sinus pressure is one-sided or bilateral.
Observe nasal discharge color and consistency over several days.

general_advice: Get plenty of rest to support airway recovery.
Drink ample warm fluids to help loosen chest secretions.
Use a cool-mist humidifier in the bedroom to keep airways moist.
Avoid respiratory irritants such as cigarette smoke, dust, and cold air.
Sip warm water with honey to calm irritating cough spasms.
when_to_seek_care: Shortness of breath, wheezing, or difficulty catching your breath.
Coughing up blood or rust-colored phlegm.
Fever higher than 38.5°C (101.3°F) or fever lasting more than 3 days.
Underlying chronic lung or heart disease (such as asthma or COPD).
monitoring_tips: Note that post-viral cough can linger for 2 to 3 weeks; watch for progressive worsening.
Monitor for any new chest tightness or wheezing.

general_advice: Identify and minimize contact with known airborne allergens like pollen, dust mites, or pet dander.
Rinse nasal passages with sterile saline to wash away trapped allergen particles.
Keep residential windows closed during high pollen count hours.
Wash face and hands and change clothes after returning from outdoors.
Use dust-mite proof covers on pillows and mattresses.
when_to_seek_care: Severe symptoms that significantly impair sleep or daytime functioning.
Development of wheezing, chest tightness, or persistent cough.
Ear pain, severe facial pain, or persistent sinus pressure.
Symptoms unresponsive to environmental avoidance measures.
monitoring_tips: Keep a simple journal tracking symptom flare-ups against outdoor activities or environmental triggers.
Notice whether symptoms are strictly seasonal or year-round.

general_advice: Sip small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solutions, clear broths, or diluted juices.
Gradually reintroduce bland foods (rice, bananas, toast, applesauce) once vomiting subsides.
Avoid dairy, greasy, highly spiced, or sugary foods until digestion settles.
Rest comfortably and allow the digestive system time to recover.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water to prevent spreading to others.
when_to_seek_care: Signs of dehydration: extreme thirst, dry mouth, little to no urination, or dark urine.
Inability to keep liquids down for more than 24 hours.
Blood in stool or vomit, or black tarry stools.
Severe, persistent abdominal pain or high fever.
monitoring_tips: Monitor frequency of fluid intake and urine output.
Watch for lightheadedness upon standing.

general_advice: Eat smaller, more frequent meals rather than large, heavy meals.
Avoid lying down for at least 2 to 3 hours after eating.
Elevate the head of your bed by 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches).
Identify and limit personal trigger foods such as fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, mint, and citrus.
Avoid tight clothing that puts pressure on the abdomen.
when_to_seek_care: Difficulty or pain when swallowing food or liquids.
Chest pain radiating to the jaw, neck, shoulder, or arm (seek immediate emergency care).
Unexplained weight loss or vomiting.
Persistent heartburn occurring multiple times weekly despite lifestyle changes.
monitoring_tips: Maintain a food and symptom diary to recognize personal dietary triggers.
Track evening meal timing relative to bedtime.

general_advice: Rest in a quiet, dark, and cool room with eyes closed.
Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the forehead or back of the neck.
Stay hydrated by sipping room-temperature water.
Limit sensory stimuli such as bright screens, loud noises, and strong odors.
Practice gentle relaxation or deep breathing techniques.
when_to_seek_care: Sudden, severe headache reaching maximum intensity in seconds ('thunderclap' headache).
Headache accompanied by fever, neck stiffness, confusion, seizures, or double vision.
Weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking that persists or is new.
New or changing headache pattern in individuals over age 50.
monitoring_tips: Keep a headache log noting duration, potential triggers (lack of sleep, missed meals, stress), and prodrome symptoms.
Record the frequency of attacks per month.

general_advice: Apply a warm heating pad or warm towel to the neck, shoulders, or back of head.
Gently stretch and massage neck, shoulder, and scalp muscles.
Take regular screen breaks using the 20-20-20 rule to reduce eye strain.
Ensure consistent sleep schedules and balanced daily hydration.
Practice mindful posture adjustments while sitting or working at a desk.
when_to_seek_care: Headache that worsens progressively over days or weeks.
Headache triggered by coughing, sneezing, or sudden movement.
Accompanying neurological symptoms like weakness or numbness.
Headaches that begin after a recent head injury.
monitoring_tips: Note workplace ergonomics, lighting conditions, and daily stress levels.
Track whether breaks and gentle stretching reduce headache intensity.

general_advice: Drink plenty of water to help flush the urinary tract.
Empty the bladder completely whenever you feel the urge to urinate.
Apply a warm heating pad across the lower abdomen to ease cramping discomfort.
Avoid bladder irritants like caffeine, alcohol, and spicy foods until symptoms clear.
Seek timely clinical evaluation for proper diagnostic confirmation and professional management.
when_to_seek_care: Fever, chills, or night sweats.
Pain in the lower back or side near the ribs (flank pain).
Visible blood in the urine or cloudy, foul-smelling urine.
Nausea and vomiting accompanying urinary discomfort.
monitoring_tips: Monitor urinary frequency and changes in urine color.
Check temperature for signs of upper urinary tract involvement.

general_advice: Drink ample water throughout the day if tolerated, aiming to maintain pale urine.
Apply a warm heating pad to the side or lower back to help soothe muscle tension.
Rest in positions of comfort that reduce strain on the back.
Seek urgent medical evaluation for severe, colicky pain and diagnostic ultrasound or imaging.
when_to_seek_care: Severe, unbearable flank or abdominal pain that does not ease.
Inability to pass urine or complete urinary blockage.
Fever and chills accompanying back or side pain.
Visible blood in the urine, persistent vomiting, or extreme lightheadedness.
monitoring_tips: Observe urine for sediment or small passed particles.
Track fluid intake and urine output volumes.

general_advice: Incorporate iron-rich foods (beans, lentils, dark leafy greens, fortified cereals, seeds) into your balanced diet.
Pair plant-based iron sources with vitamin C rich foods (citrus fruits, bell peppers) to support absorption.
Limit consumption of tea and coffee during meals, as tannins can hinder iron uptake.
Pace daily activities to conserve energy and take short rest breaks when fatigued.
Consult a doctor for appropriate blood tests before considering supplements.
when_to_seek_care: Chest discomfort, heart palpitations, or shortness of breath during routine activities.
Severe dizziness, fainting spells, or confusion.
Unusually heavy menstrual bleeding or visible blood in stool.
Pale skin accompanied by persistent extreme weakness.
monitoring_tips: Notice energy levels throughout the day and how exertion affects stamina.
Discuss periodic blood checkups with your doctor.

general_advice: Adopt a balanced, whole-foods diet emphasizing fiber, vegetables, and complex carbohydrates while moderating refined sugars.
Engage in regular, gentle physical activity like daily brisk walking as appropriate.
Stay well hydrated with plain water and unsweetened beverages.
Inspect feet daily for cuts, blisters, redness, or swelling.
Schedule a clinical evaluation for comprehensive metabolic blood testing and professional guidance.
when_to_seek_care: Frequent excessive urination accompanied by unquenchable thirst, nausea, and rapid breathing.
Confusion, fruity-smelling breath, or persistent vomiting.
Cuts, sores, or skin infections on the feet or legs that are slow to heal.
Sudden blurred vision or loss of sensation in fingers or toes.
monitoring_tips: Keep a log of fasting blood glucose readings if using a home glucometer.
Record daily meals and physical activity patterns.

general_advice: Apply a clean, cool or warm damp compress over closed eyelids to soothe irritation.
Avoid rubbing or touching your eyes to prevent exacerbating inflammation or spreading.
Wash hands thoroughly and often with soap and water.
Use a fresh clean washcloth and towel each time, and do not share towels or pillowcases.
Temporarily discontinue contact lens wear until symptoms resolve and a professional clears lens use.
when_to_seek_care: Moderate to severe eye pain, or extreme sensitivity to light (photophobia).
Changes in vision, such as blurriness or halos around lights.
Copious yellow or green discharge causing eyelids to stick shut.
Symptoms that do not improve after 48 to 72 hours.
monitoring_tips: Observe whether one or both eyes are involved.
Notice whether discharge is watery or thick.

general_advice: Stay gently active; avoid prolonged strict bed rest, which can prolong stiffness.
Apply ice packs wrapped in a cloth for the first 48 hours, followed by warm compresses to relax muscles.
Perform gentle walking on level surfaces and light lower-back stretches as tolerated.
Maintain ergonomic seating with lumbar support and avoid heavy lifting or sudden twisting.
Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees, or on your back with a pillow under your knees.
when_to_seek_care: Loss of bowel or bladder control (cauda equina warning sign — seek emergency care immediately).
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the groin, inner thighs ('saddle anesthesia'), or legs.
Back pain accompanied by unexplained fever or unexplained weight loss.
Severe pain following a fall, accident, or physical trauma.
monitoring_tips: Monitor mobility changes and walking tolerance over a few days.
Note specific positions that relieve or aggravate the discomfort.

general_advice: Maintain strict bed rest and avoid strenuous physical activity.
Drink abundant fluids (oral rehydration solution, coconut water, fresh clear broths) to counteract plasma leakage.
Use mosquito nets and repellents to prevent transmission to household members.
Use a cool, damp cloth on the forehead to provide comfort during fever spikes.
Seek timely medical care and regular platelet count monitoring from a qualified healthcare facility.
when_to_seek_care: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness.
Persistent vomiting (at least 3 episodes in 24 hours).
Bleeding from gums or nose, blood in vomit or stools, or red spots on skin (petechiae).
Lethargy, restlessness, difficulty breathing, or cold, clammy skin.
monitoring_tips: Watch for warning signs especially as fever begins to break (the critical phase, days 3 to 7).
Ensure regular hydration and record daily fluid intake and urination.

general_advice: Seek immediate clinical evaluation and blood smear or rapid diagnostic testing.
Rest quietly in bed during shivering chills and high fever cycles.
Drink ample fluids including oral rehydration solutions to prevent dehydration from heavy sweating.
Sponge with lukewarm water during fever spikes to promote comfort.
Sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets to protect family and community members.
when_to_seek_care: Severe drowsiness, confusion, convulsions, or inability to stay awake.
Rapid or labored breathing.
Yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice).
Dark or tea-colored urine.
monitoring_tips: Record the timing and cycle of fever spikes and chills.
Note any international or regional travel to malaria-endemic regions.

general_advice: Seek formal clinical evaluation for blood culture, Widal test, or appropriate diagnostic confirmation.
Drink only boiled, filtered, or commercially bottled water.
Consume freshly cooked, soft, easily digestible foods like porridge, boiled potatoes, and clear broths.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before eating and after using the restroom.
Ensure complete bed rest while body temperature fluctuates.
when_to_seek_care: Severe, persistent abdominal pain or abdominal distension.
Bleeding from the rectum, black stools, or severe diarrhea.
High sustained fever unresponsive to cooling measures.
Confusion, apathy, extreme weakness, or hallucinations.
monitoring_tips: Log temperature daily at morning and evening.
Track bowel movement frequency and stool appearance.

general_advice: Prioritize rest and avoid heavy load-bearing on swollen or painful joints.
Apply cold packs wrapped in a cloth to painful, swollen joints for 15-minute intervals.
Drink plenty of water and electrolyte solutions to prevent dehydration.
Perform gentle passive range-of-motion exercises once acute joint swelling eases.
Use mosquito protection measures like netting and screens to prevent spread.
when_to_seek_care: Extreme joint pain preventing any weight-bearing or self-care.
Persistent high fever lasting more than 5 days.
Drowsiness, confusion, or neck stiffness.
Severe vomiting or decreased urine output.
monitoring_tips: Track which joints are affected and whether swelling is symmetrical.
Note morning joint stiffness duration.

general_advice: Seek prompt clinical evaluation at a specialized healthcare center for sputum and chest imaging.
Rest in well-ventilated rooms with open windows to facilitate fresh air circulation.
Cover mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, and dispose of tissues safely.
Maintain a nutrient-dense, high-protein diet to support immune recovery.
Follow licensed physician directions diligently and attend all scheduled clinical follow-ups.
when_to_seek_care: Coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum (hemoptysis).
Sudden chest pain or severe breathlessness.
Rapid, unexplained weight loss and drenching night sweats.
High persistent fever.
monitoring_tips: Track weight changes weekly.
Note the duration of cough (especially if exceeding 2 to 3 weeks).

general_advice: Ensure complete physical bed rest, particularly during the acute fatigue phase.
Eat small, frequent, light meals high in complex carbohydrates to combat nausea.
Drink plenty of clean, safe water and fruit juices to remain hydrated.
Strictly avoid alcohol and unapproved herbal concoctions to protect liver function.
Practice diligent hand hygiene after restroom use and before handling food.
when_to_seek_care: Progressive yellowing of skin or eyes (deepening jaundice).
Severe, intractable vomiting preventing any fluid retention.
Unusual bruising, bleeding from gums, or confusion and disorientation.
Extreme abdominal swelling or severe right upper quadrant pain.
monitoring_tips: Observe changes in urine color (dark tea-colored) and stool color (pale or clay-colored).
Record daily energy levels and appetite.

general_advice: Apply fragrance-free moisturizers or emollients immediately after bathing to lock in moisture.
Take short lukewarm showers or baths (under 10 minutes) using gentle, soap-free cleansers.
Wear loose, breathable cotton clothing and avoid scratchy wool or synthetic fabrics.
Keep fingernails short and clean to minimize skin damage from involuntary scratching.
Apply cool compresses over intensely itchy patches to provide soothing relief.
when_to_seek_care: Signs of secondary bacterial skin infection: honey-colored crusting, pus, warmth, or red streaks.
Widespread, intensely painful rash or rash accompanied by fever.
Eczema flare-up that severely disrupts sleep or daily activities.
Symptoms that do not improve with regular moisturizing.
monitoring_tips: Identify common flare triggers like harsh detergents, sweat, dry weather, or emotional stress.
Assess skin barrier hydration morning and night.

general_advice: Keep the affected skin area clean, cool, and thoroughly dry.
Wear loose-fitting, breathable cotton clothing and change clothes daily.
Avoid sharing towels, combs, bedding, or personal grooming items with others.
Wash hands thoroughly after touching affected areas to prevent spreading.
Disinfect surfaces and shower areas regularly.
when_to_seek_care: Rash that spreads rapidly, becomes increasingly red, warm, or swollen.
Pus-filled blisters or open sores developing within the rash.
Infection affecting the scalp, beard, or extensive body areas.
No noticeable improvement after two weeks of good hygiene.
monitoring_tips: Observe the outer expanding border of the rash.
Ensure skin folds and webbed areas between toes are patted completely dry after washing.

general_advice: Apply cool, damp washcloths to itchy areas to soothe burning or stinging sensations.
Wear loose, lightweight cotton clothing to avoid friction and skin irritation.
Take cool or lukewarm baths; avoid hot showers, which can trigger histamine release.
Avoid scratching the welts, which can worsen swelling and trigger new hives.
Identify and avoid suspected acute triggers like sudden temperature shifts, stress, or specific foods.
when_to_seek_care: Swelling of the lips, tongue, throat, or face (angioedema — seek emergency care immediately).
Difficulty breathing, throat tightness, or wheezing.
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint.
Hives lasting continuously for longer than 6 weeks.
monitoring_tips: Keep a log of exposures prior to hive outbreaks (foods, cosmetics, heat, pressure).
Note how long individual welts last (typical acute hives fade in under 24 hours in one spot).

general_advice: Seek formal clinical evaluation for accurate microscopic examination and appropriate medical treatment.
Wash all bedding, towels, and recently worn clothes in hot water and dry on high heat.
Items that cannot be washed should be sealed in an airtight plastic bag for at least 3 to 7 days.
Clip fingernails short to prevent skin excoriation from intense nighttime itching.
Household members and close contacts should be evaluated simultaneously to prevent re-infestation.
when_to_seek_care: Signs of secondary bacterial skin infection (oozing sores, expanding redness, pustules).
Severe crusted lesions or involvement of large skin surface areas.
Severe itching unresponsive to initial medical care.
Infants, elderly, or immunocompromised individuals presenting with widespread rash.
monitoring_tips: Look for classic burrows in skin folds (between fingers, wrists, armpits, waistline).
Note that post-treatment itching can persist for several weeks as the skin heals.

general_advice: Wash face gently twice daily with a mild, non-drying cleanser and lukewarm water.
Avoid picking, squeezing, or popping pimples, which increases inflammation and scarring risk.
Choose non-comedogenic (oil-free) moisturizers, sunscreen, and skincare products.
Wash hair regularly and keep hair away from touching the face.
Rinse face after exercising or sweating heavily.
when_to_seek_care: Deep, painful cysts or nodules beneath the skin.
Acne resulting in noticeable scarring or dark hyperpigmentation.
Acne accompanied by sudden excessive facial hair growth or irregular menstrual cycles.
Persistent breakout unresponsive to consistent gentle skincare over 8 to 12 weeks.
monitoring_tips: Allow 4 to 8 weeks to evaluate whether a gentle skincare routine shows effect.
Notice whether dietary patterns or cosmetic products correlate with breakouts.

general_advice: Rest comfortably at home and isolate from others until all blisters have fully crusted over.
Apply cool, wet compresses or take lukewarm baths with colloidal oatmeal to relieve itching.
Wear loose, smooth cotton clothing to minimize friction against healing blisters.
Keep fingernails trimmed short and clean, or wear soft cotton gloves at night to prevent scratching.
Drink plenty of cool fluids and eat soft, non-acidic foods if mouth sores are present.
when_to_seek_care: Rash spreading into the eyes or surrounding eye skin.
Blisters that become unusually red, warm, tender, or leak thick yellow pus.
Extreme drowsiness, confusion, unsteady walking, or persistent high fever.
Difficulty breathing, persistent cough, or severe chest pain.
monitoring_tips: Count days until all lesions have scabbed over (usually 5 to 7 days after first spots appear).
Check temperature regularly and monitor for skin infections.

general_advice: Seek prompt clinical medical evaluation for appropriate clinical assessment and care.
Elevate the affected limb above the level of the heart to help reduce swelling.
Rest the affected area and avoid strenuous physical movement.
Gently outline the visible red border on the skin with a clean pen to monitor if spreading.
Keep the skin clean and dry, protecting any underlying cuts with a clean dressing.
when_to_seek_care: Rapidly expanding redness, warmth, or swelling beyond marked borders.
Fever, chills, shivering, nausea, or rapid heartbeat.
Blistering, purple discoloration, or skin breakdown in the affected area.
Cellulitis near the eyes, face, or in individuals with diabetes or poor circulation.
monitoring_tips: Check the drawn pen border every 4 to 6 hours for signs of expansion.
Monitor body temperature for fever spikes.

general_advice: Call emergency medical services (112 or local emergency number) immediately.
Rest in a comfortable, seated position while waiting for emergency responders; do not walk or exert yourself.
Loosen any tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist.
Do not drive yourself to the hospital; await an ambulance equipped for cardiac care.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for any suspected cardiac event.
Chest pressure, squeezing, fullness, or pain radiating to jaw, neck, back, or arms.
Shortness of breath, cold sweat, lightheadedness, or sudden unexplained nausea.
monitoring_tips: Do not wait to see if symptoms pass; early medical intervention is vital.
Have someone stay with the person until medical personnel arrive.

general_advice: Call emergency medical services (112 or local emergency number) immediately.
Remember the FAST test: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency.
Keep the person calm, lying down with head and shoulders slightly elevated.
Do not give the person anything to eat, drink, or swallow.
Record the exact time when symptoms were first noticed.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately at the first sign of stroke.
Sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body.
Sudden confusion, difficulty speaking, or difficulty understanding speech.
Sudden vision trouble, loss of balance, or severe thunderclap headache.
monitoring_tips: Note exact time of symptom onset for medical teams (critical for time-sensitive treatments).
Remain with the patient continuously.

general_advice: Seek emergency medical evaluation at a hospital emergency department immediately.
Do not eat or drink anything in case surgical evaluation is required.
Do not apply heat pads to the abdomen, which may exacerbate internal inflammation.
Do not take laxatives or enemas, which can increase risk of appendix rupture.
Rest quietly in a comfortable position with knees drawn up while traveling for medical care.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate emergency hospital care for sharp or worsening lower right abdominal pain.
Pain that began around the navel and migrated to the right lower abdomen.
Abdominal pain accompanied by fever, vomiting, and inability to pass gas.
Sudden relief of pain followed by widespread severe abdominal tenderness (possible perforation).
monitoring_tips: Avoid taking food or water while en route to medical evaluation.
Note the progression of abdominal pain location and intensity.

general_advice: Call emergency medical services (112 or local emergency number) immediately.
If an epinephrine auto-injector is available and prescribed for the individual, use it without delay.
Help the person lie flat with legs elevated, unless breathing is difficult, in which case keep sitting.
Loosen tight clothing and keep the person warm with a blanket.
Do not give anything by mouth.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for all suspected anaphylactic events.
Swelling of the throat, lips, tongue, or difficulty breathing.
Sudden widespread hives accompanied by dizziness, fainting, or rapid pulse.
Nausea, abdominal cramping, or vomiting following exposure to an allergen.
monitoring_tips: A second wave of symptoms (biphasic reaction) can occur hours later; hospital observation is essential.
Note the suspected allergen (food, insect sting, medication).

general_advice: Seek emergency medical evaluation at the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Do not delay seeking clinical care for suspected meningitis.
Rest in a quiet, darkened room while awaiting emergency transport.
Keep the head and neck in a neutral, relaxed position.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate emergency hospital care.
Sudden high fever combined with severe headache and stiff, painful neck.
Sensitivity to light (photophobia), confusion, altered mental state, or drowsiness.
New non-blanching dark purple or red skin rash (does not fade under a clear drinking glass).
monitoring_tips: Check if skin rash fades under gentle pressure with a clear glass.
Ensure continuous supervision while emergency medical care is arranged.

general_advice: Sit upright comfortably and try to take slow, steady breaths.
Move away from known environmental triggers such as smoke, cold air, dust, or pet dander.
Follow your personal written asthma action plan agreed upon with your healthcare provider.
Stay calm, as anxiety can heighten feelings of breathlessness.
Ensure your prescribed reliever inhaler is readily accessible.
when_to_seek_care: Severe breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences without pausing for breath.
Chest and neck muscles pulling in tightly during breathing (retractions).
Reliever inhaler not providing relief or needing to be used more frequently than prescribed.
Bluish or gray discoloration of lips, face, or fingernails (emergency).
monitoring_tips: Track peak flow readings if using a home peak flow meter.
Record how often symptoms require daytime or nighttime reliever use.

general_advice: Seek comprehensive clinical medical evaluation for stethoscope examination, chest imaging, and care.
Get plenty of bed rest to allow your lungs and immune system to heal.
Drink ample warm fluids, teas, and broths to keep hydrated and thin chest mucus.
Use a cool-mist humidifier or sit in a steamy bathroom to ease breathing comfort.
Avoid tobacco smoke, secondhand smoke, and other lung irritants.
when_to_seek_care: Difficulty breathing, shortness of breath at rest, or rapid shallow breathing.
Chest pain that sharpens when breathing in or coughing.
Coughing up blood or dark greenish/brownish phlegm.
Persistent high fever, confusion, or bluish lips or fingertips.
monitoring_tips: Monitor body temperature and resting respiratory rate.
Check oxygen saturation with a home pulse oximeter if available.

general_advice: Call emergency medical services (112 or local emergency number) immediately.
Move the person to a cool, shaded, or air-conditioned environment right away.
Cool the body rapidly: immerse in cool water, spray with cool water, or apply ice packs wrapped in towels to neck, armpits, and groin.
Fan the person while misting skin with cool water.
Do not give fluids if the person is confused, vomiting, or semi-conscious.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for heat stroke (a medical emergency).
High body temperature (40°C / 104°F or higher).
Altered mental state, confusion, slurred speech, delirium, seizures, or coma.
Hot, red, dry skin or heavy sweating that abruptly stops.
monitoring_tips: Continue active cooling until emergency personnel arrive.
Check breathing and level of consciousness continuously.
